[Findings](/findings/index.md) / UX-056

# Scrolling back up a little puts focus in the address bar and opens the keyboard

Open · high severity · failure · Firefox on iPad

## What we saw

Reading a long page, a small scroll back up brings the hidden toolbars back, the address field gets focus with its URL selected, and the on-screen keyboard opens over the bottom half of the page (second screenshot: the URL selected, Cancel showing, the keyboard covering the release table). Nothing on the page was tapped on purpose. A likely mechanism, not yet confirmed: the toolbar slides in under the finger mid-gesture, so the touch that was a scroll lands on the address field as a tap.

![Firefox on iPad after a small scroll up: the tab strip and address bar are back, the URL is selected for editing and the keyboard covers the lower half of the newsroom release history](/findings/img/UX-056-keyboard-after-scroll-up.webp)

_After a small scroll up: address field focused, URL selected, keyboard open. Nothing on the page was tapped._

## Why it matters

The reader was not asking to go anywhere, and loses half the screen to a keyboard. Worse, it looks like the page has a bug: the first reading was that the site had somehow started an edit. The browser's fault is charged to the site, and the reader's concentration is broken either way.

## The fix

For the browser: a scroll gesture never focuses the address field; only a deliberate tap on a toolbar that is already at rest does. For the sites: nothing a page can prevent, but worth knowing that readers will report it as our bug, so it is recorded here with its real owner.

## The record

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | Open |
| **Severity** | High |
| **Kind** | Failure: works against the reader |
| **Product** | [Firefox on iPad](/findings/?product=firefox-ipad), browser |
| **Where** | <https://newsroom.sgit.ai/admin/versions.html> |
| **Problems** | [Focus hijack](/findings/?problem=focus-hijack), [Unexpected movement](/findings/?problem=unexpected-movement), [Wrong culprit](/findings/?problem=wrong-culprit) |
| **Visibility** | [Intermittent](/findings/?visibility=intermittent): some readers, some of the time: depends on a gesture, a device or a state, and is hard to reproduce on demand |
| **Recommendation** | [Keep the UI still](/findings/?recommendation=keep-the-ui-still): nothing moves, appears or takes focus unless the reader asked for it; chrome that hides stays hidden until a deliberate gesture |
| **Area** | [Navigation](/findings/?area=navigation) |
| **Breaks** | [Nothing moves that the reader did not move](/principles/index.md#ui-stays-still) |
| **Observed** | 2026-10-18, not recorded |
| **Last checked** | 2026-10-18, not recorded |
| **Environment** | Firefox for iOS on an iPad, landscape, reading newsroom.sgit.ai/admin/versions.html (newsroom v0.12.120) |
| **Source** | [Reported by Dinis Cruz, 18 Oct 2026, with screenshots](/method/index.md#reports-from-readers) |

[Findings](/findings/index.md) / UX-057

# The toolbars come back on any small scroll up, taking screen and moving the page

Open · medium severity · failure · Firefox on iPad

## What we saw

Scrolled down, Firefox shows only a thin address line and the page gets almost the whole screen (first screenshot: the newsroom header starts about 90 px down a 1,640 px screen). Any small scroll up restores the tab strip and full address bar (second screenshot: the header starts about 270 px down), about 180 px or 11% of the screen, and the page content shifts down by that much while it is being read. The hidden state is the one wanted all the time. What brings them back is not the distance scrolled: see UX-058 for how they are hidden, which depends on the speed of the gesture.

![Firefox on iPad scrolled down: only a thin address line above the newsroom header, the release history filling the screen](/findings/img/UX-057-toolbar-hidden.webp)

_Scrolled down: toolbars collapsed to a thin address line. This is the state wanted all the time._

![The same page after a small scroll up, with the tab strip and address bar back](/findings/img/UX-056-keyboard-after-scroll-up.webp)

_After a small scroll up: tab strip and address bar back, the page pushed down about 180 px (and, here, the keyboard too: UX-056)._

## Why it matters

The reader scrolls up a line to re-read a sentence and the whole page jumps, the text moves away from their eyes, and a toolbar they did not ask for takes a ninth of the screen. Each time, attention goes to the chrome instead of the text.

## The fix

For the browser: keep the toolbars hidden until a deliberate gesture (a tap on the address line, or a scroll to the very top), and offer a setting to keep them collapsed. For the sites, on our side of the line: keep our own sticky header as small as it can be, because it stacks on top of the browser's (on this page the newsroom's header takes about another 110 px).

**What good looks like:** [EX-001 Safari on iPad hides its toolbars the same way every time, after a small scroll](/exemplars/EX-001.md).

## The record

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | Open |
| **Severity** | Medium |
| **Kind** | Failure: works against the reader |
| **Product** | [Firefox on iPad](/findings/?product=firefox-ipad), browser |
| **Where** | <https://newsroom.sgit.ai/admin/versions.html> |
| **Problems** | [Unexpected movement](/findings/?problem=unexpected-movement), [Lost screen space](/findings/?problem=lost-screen-space) |
| **Visibility** | [Obvious](/findings/?visibility=obvious): every reader sees it, every time they reach that point |
| **Recommendation** | [Keep the UI still](/findings/?recommendation=keep-the-ui-still): nothing moves, appears or takes focus unless the reader asked for it; chrome that hides stays hidden until a deliberate gesture |
| **Area** | [Navigation](/findings/?area=navigation) |
| **Breaks** | [Nothing moves that the reader did not move](/principles/index.md#ui-stays-still) |
| **Observed** | 2026-10-18, not recorded |
| **Last checked** | 2026-10-18, not recorded |
| **Environment** | Firefox for iOS on an iPad, landscape, reading newsroom.sgit.ai/admin/versions.html (newsroom v0.12.120) |
| **Source** | [Reported by Dinis Cruz, 18 Oct 2026, with screenshots](/method/index.md#reports-from-readers) |

[Findings](/findings/index.md) / UX-058

# Whether the toolbars hide depends on how fast you scroll, not how far

Open · medium severity · failure · Firefox on iPad

## What we saw

Dragging the page up slowly, by any distance, leaves the full toolbars in place: tab strip, address bar, about 230 px of a 1,640 px screen before the page starts (first screenshot). A flick hides them, leaving a thin address line (second screenshot), but a flick also scrolls the page by an amount the reader does not control, so it overshoots. Scrolling back to the place wanted risks the small upward scroll that brings the toolbars back (UX-057) and can focus the address bar (UX-056). It is hard to reproduce on demand because it depends on gesture speed.

![Firefox on iPad at the top of the newsroom front page after a slow scroll: the tab strip and full address bar take the top of the screen](/findings/img/UX-058-toolbars-full.webp)

_After a slow drag: the full toolbars stay, however far the page has moved._

![The same front page after a flick: only a thin address line above the newsroom header, the page scrolled well past where the reader was](/findings/img/UX-058-toolbars-collapsed-after-flick.webp)

_After a flick: the toolbars hide, and the page has scrolled past where the reader was._

## Why it matters

The reader cannot ask for the state they want. To read with the toolbars hidden they have to flick, lose their place, find it again carefully, and hope the correction does not undo the result. Every attempt takes attention away from the text, which is the opposite of what hiding the toolbars is for.

## The fix

For the browser: make the toolbar state depend on something the reader controls (distance scrolled, or a deliberate tap on the address line), the same every time, and offer a setting to keep the toolbars collapsed while reading. For the sites: nothing a page can do about the browser's chrome; keep our own sticky header small, since it is the part of the stack we own.

**What good looks like:** [EX-001 Safari on iPad hides its toolbars the same way every time, after a small scroll](/exemplars/EX-001.md).

## The record

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | Open |
| **Severity** | Medium |
| **Kind** | Failure: works against the reader |
| **Product** | [Firefox on iPad](/findings/?product=firefox-ipad), browser |
| **Where** | <https://newsroom.sgit.ai/> |
| **Problems** | [Unpredictable control](/findings/?problem=unpredictable-control), [Unexpected movement](/findings/?problem=unexpected-movement), [Lost screen space](/findings/?problem=lost-screen-space) |
| **Visibility** | [Intermittent](/findings/?visibility=intermittent): some readers, some of the time: depends on a gesture, a device or a state, and is hard to reproduce on demand |
| **Recommendation** | [Make it predictable](/findings/?recommendation=make-it-predictable): the same gesture always gives the same result, and the reader can set the state directly instead of coaxing it |
| **Area** | [Navigation](/findings/?area=navigation) |
| **Breaks** | [The same gesture gives the same result, so it can be learned](/principles/index.md#same-gesture-same-result) |
| **Observed** | 2026-10-18, not recorded |
| **Last checked** | 2026-10-18, not recorded |
| **Environment** | Firefox for iOS on an iPad, landscape, on the newsroom.sgit.ai front page (newsroom v0.12.120) |
| **Source** | [Reported by Dinis Cruz, 18 Oct 2026, with screenshots](/method/index.md#reports-from-readers) |

[Findings](/findings/index.md) / UX-059

# A security prompt that asks you to approve a command it does not explain, and cuts off

Open · high severity · failure · Claude app (iPhone and iPad)

## What we saw

The prompt says only "Bash wants to run:" above a box of raw shell: a variable holding a long path, then python3 reading a heredoc that rewrites a line in two files (tools/partition.py and tools/site_gate.py). Lines wrap mid-word ("newsro / om", "repos / itory") and the box is cut off with a fade halfway through the line that matters, the replacement string; nothing says whether it scrolls. Above it, a lock icon and its padding take about a quarter of the prompt. Below, two buttons, Deny and a filled black Allow once, which is the visually stronger choice. Nothing on the prompt says, in words, what the command does, which files it changes, whether it touches the network, whether it can be undone, or connects it to the agent's own explanation in the conversation behind the prompt ("team repo records need to move to records/").

![Claude app on iPhone showing a permission prompt: a lock icon, "Bash wants to run:", a box of raw shell and Python cut off with a fade mid-line, and Deny and Allow once buttons](/findings/img/UX-059-bash-permission-prompt.webp)

_The prompt as shown: raw code, wrapped mid-word and cut off mid-line, with no plain-words summary of what it will do._

## Why it matters

The person is asked to make a security decision and given only code to make it with, partly hidden, on a phone. In practice the choice is to stop the work or to trust blindly, and every prompt like this teaches the habit of pressing Allow without reading, which defeats the point of asking. Here the command was harmless (a one-line edit to two files), but the prompt would have looked the same if it were not.

## The fix

Lead with one line in plain words: "Edit 2 files in the newsroom repository: tools/partition.py and tools/site_gate.py (one line each)". Then the facts that decide it, as labels: reads, writes, deletes, network, outside the working directory, reversible. For an edit, show the diff, not the script that makes it. Link the agent's stated reason. Keep the full command one tap away, with real line breaks and no mid-word wrapping. Give Deny and Allow equal weight, or emphasise the safe choice. The short description already exists: the Bash tool asks the agent for a plain-words description of every command it runs, and the prompt does not show it.

## The record

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | Open |
| **Severity** | High |
| **Kind** | Failure: works against the reader |
| **Product** | [Claude app (iPhone and iPad)](/findings/?product=claude-app-ios), app |
| **Where** | Claude Code session, Bash permission prompt |
| **Problems** | [Uninformed decision](/findings/?problem=uninformed-decision), [Buried content](/findings/?problem=buried-content), [Missing signal](/findings/?problem=missing-signal) |
| **Visibility** | [Obvious](/findings/?visibility=obvious): every reader sees it, every time they reach that point |
| **Recommendation** | [Explain the decision](/findings/?recommendation=explain-the-decision): before asking, say in plain words what will happen, what it touches, whether it can be undone and why it is being asked, with the raw detail one tap away |
| **Area** | [Security decisions](/findings/?area=security) |
| **Breaks** | [A decision comes with what you need to make it](/principles/index.md#informed-decisions) |
| **Observed** | 2026-10-25, not recorded |
| **Last checked** | 2026-10-25, not recorded |
| **Environment** | Claude app on iPhone, portrait, supervising a remote Claude Code session working on the newsroom repository |
| **Source** | [Reported by Dinis Cruz, 25 Oct 2026, with a screenshot](/method/index.md#reports-from-readers) |

[Findings](/findings/index.md) / UX-060

# One unlabelled X throws away the whole recording, with no confirmation

Open · high severity · failure · Claude app (iPhone and iPad)

## What we saw

While dictating, the message box shows three buttons: an X on the left, a square and an up arrow on the right. None is labelled. The X discards the recording and its transcript at once: no "discard this recording?", no undo, no copy kept. It sits where a "close" or "minimise" usually sits.

![Claude app on iPad while dictating: the transcript so far in the message box, a waveform, an X button on the left, a square button and an orange up-arrow button side by side on the right, none of them labelled](/findings/img/UX-060-voice-input-controls.webp)

_The three controls while dictating: X (discards everything, no confirmation), square (stops and lets you edit), up arrow (sends as is). None is labelled._

## Why it matters

A minute of dictation, often the hardest part of the message, is gone in one tap, on the button that looks least consequential. It has already happened to the reporter: "I literally fell for this in the past."

## The fix

Ask before discarding a recording longer than a few seconds, or discard with an undo ("Recording discarded · Undo") and keep the audio for a while. Label it "Discard". Move it away from the corner people tap to dismiss things.

## The record

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | Open |
| **Severity** | High |
| **Kind** | Failure: works against the reader |
| **Product** | [Claude app (iPhone and iPad)](/findings/?product=claude-app-ios), app |
| **Where** | Message box, voice input |
| **Problems** | [Data loss](/findings/?problem=data-loss), [Unlabelled](/findings/?problem=unlabelled) |
| **Visibility** | [Obvious](/findings/?visibility=obvious): every reader sees it, every time they reach that point |
| **Recommendation** | [Confirm or undo](/findings/?recommendation=confirm-or-undo): a destructive action either asks first or can be undone, and the safe choice is the easy one |
| **Area** | [Input and dictation](/findings/?area=input) |
| **Breaks** | [Work is never lost to one tap or a silent failure](/principles/index.md#work-is-never-lost) |
| **Observed** | 2026-10-25, not recorded |
| **Last checked** | 2026-10-25, not recorded |
| **Environment** | Claude app on iPad, landscape, dictating a message into a Claude Code session |
| **Source** | [Reported by Dinis Cruz, 25 Oct 2026, by voice, with a screenshot](/method/index.md#reports-from-readers) |

[Findings](/findings/index.md) / UX-061

# Three voice controls with no labels: the safe one and the send-as-is one sit side by side

Open · medium severity · failure · Claude app (iPhone and iPad)

## What we saw

Of the three buttons, the square is the one you usually want: it stops recording and puts the transcript in the box to correct, which dictated text nearly always needs. The up arrow, right next to it, sends the transcript as is, uncorrected. Nothing (label, tooltip, first-use hint) says which does what; the reporter learned all three by trial and error.

![Claude app on iPad while dictating: the transcript so far in the message box, a waveform, an X button on the left, a square button and an orange up-arrow button side by side on the right, none of them labelled](/findings/img/UX-060-voice-input-controls.webp)

_The square (stop and edit) and the up arrow (send as is) are adjacent and unlabelled._

## Why it matters

Every first use is a guess, and the guess has consequences: a wrong tap either destroys the recording (UX-060) or sends a message full of transcription errors to an agent that will act on it.

## The fix

Label the buttons ("Discard", "Stop and edit", "Send"), at least until they have been used a few times. Make "Stop and edit" the visually primary action, and put space between it and "Send".

## The record

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | Open |

| **Kind** | Failure: works against the reader |
| **Product** | [Claude app (iPhone and iPad)](/findings/?product=claude-app-ios), app |
| **Where** | Message box, voice input |
| **Problems** | [Unlabelled](/findings/?problem=unlabelled), [Uninformed decision](/findings/?problem=uninformed-decision) |
| **Visibility** | [Obvious](/findings/?visibility=obvious): every reader sees it, every time they reach that point |
| **Recommendation** | [Say what it is](/findings/?recommendation=say-what-it-is): label it, in the reader's terms, at the moment it matters |
| **Area** | [Input and dictation](/findings/?area=input) |
| **Breaks** | [A decision comes with what you need to make it](/principles/index.md#informed-decisions) |

[Findings](/findings/index.md) / UX-062

# The transcript is cleaned up in a second pass without saying when, or what changed

Open · low severity · failure · Claude app (iPhone and iPad)

## What we saw

After the live transcript, a second pass rewrites the text to tidy it up. The result is usually better, but nothing shows that it happened, when it happened, or which words were changed from what was actually said.

## Why it matters

The reader can no longer tell their own words from the model's interpretation of them, so they cannot tell what to check. For an instruction to an agent, a quietly changed word can change the task.

## The fix

Mark the moment the second pass runs, highlight words it changed, and offer "show what I said" or a one-tap revert to the raw transcript.

## The record

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | Open |
| **Severity** | Low |
| **Kind** | Failure: works against the reader |
| **Product** | [Claude app (iPhone and iPad)](/findings/?product=claude-app-ios), app |
| **Where** | Message box, voice input |
| **Problems** | [Silent change](/findings/?problem=silent-change) |
| **Visibility** | [Subtle](/findings/?visibility=subtle): felt more than seen: it costs attention or trust, but is not noticed as a bug |
| **Recommendation** | [Show what changed](/findings/?recommendation=show-what-changed): when the system rewrites what the reader made, mark it, and let them see and undo the change |
| **Area** | [Input and dictation](/findings/?area=input) |
| **Breaks** | [Say who wrote it, and how](/principles/index.md#say-who-wrote-it) |
| **Observed** | 2026-10-25, not recorded |
| **Last checked** | 2026-10-25, not recorded |
| **Environment** | Claude app on iPad, landscape, dictating a message into a Claude Code session |

[Findings](/findings/index.md) / UX-063

# The live transcript sometimes stops while you are still speaking, and nothing says whether it is still recording

Open · high severity · failure · Claude app (iPhone and iPad)

## What we saw

Mid-dictation the live transcript can stop updating while the waveform keeps moving, so there is no way to know whether the rest is being captured. Sometimes pressing the square then shows the missing text after a "transcribing" step; sometimes it has been lost. The reporter puts it at roughly half the time it stalls, and has lost "quite a lot of voice memos" this way. The audio is never offered back for a retry.

![Claude app on iPad while dictating: the transcript so far in the message box, a waveform, an X button on the left, a square button and an orange up-arrow button side by side on the right, none of them labelled](/findings/img/UX-060-voice-input-controls.webp)

_Mid-dictation: the transcript ends at "usability" while the waveform keeps moving. Is the rest being recorded? Nothing says._

## Why it matters

The reader has to keep a mental check running while they speak, watching for words to appear, and stops trusting the tool whenever they do not. When it fails the recording cannot be recovered or resubmitted, so the loss is total.

## The fix

Show the state explicitly: "Live transcript paused, audio still recording" when the live pass stalls, and a clear error if capture itself stops. Keep the audio on the device until the final transcript is in the box, and offer "Transcribe again" when it fails.

**What good looks like:** [EX-002 Dictation that shows your words as you speak them](/exemplars/EX-002.md).

## The record

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | Open |
| **Severity** | High |
| **Kind** | Failure: works against the reader |
| **Product** | [Claude app (iPhone and iPad)](/findings/?product=claude-app-ios), app |
| **Where** | Message box, voice input |
| **Problems** | [Missing feedback](/findings/?problem=missing-feedback), [Data loss](/findings/?problem=data-loss) |
| **Visibility** | [Intermittent](/findings/?visibility=intermittent): some readers, some of the time: depends on a gesture, a device or a state, and is hard to reproduce on demand |
| **Recommendation** | [Show the state](/findings/?recommendation=show-the-state): always show what the system is doing (listening, working, paused, failed) and keep what was captured until it is safely delivered |
| **Area** | [Input and dictation](/findings/?area=input) |
| **Breaks** | [The reader can always tell what the system is doing](/principles/index.md#system-state-is-visible) |
| **Observed** | 2026-10-25, not recorded |
| **Last checked** | 2026-10-25, not recorded |
| **Environment** | Claude app on iPad, landscape, dictating a message into a Claude Code session |
| **Source** | [Reported by Dinis Cruz, 25 Oct 2026, by voice, with a screenshot](/method/index.md#reports-from-readers) |

# Findings

Every UX failure and gap in the register, open first, then by severity. A **failure** works against the reader; a **gap** is something the reader needs that is not there. Each status says when it was last checked, and on which version: nothing here claims to be current beyond that.

## How a finding gets here

Someone uses the site as a stranger would: a phone, a link, three minutes. What gets in their way is written down with the evidence, the date and the version, then named against a [principle](/principles/index.md). The [method](/method/index.md) has the details. The first source was the [newsroom UX review of 11 October 2026](/reviews/newsroom-2026-10-11.md); new findings come from the same kind of look at any site in the network.

By Dinis Cruz, written with AI agents. [Why this exists](/about/index.md). This site follows its own principles, or it is a finding too: the first screen says what it is, every view is a link, every count is generated from [one file](/data/findings.json), and the content is there without JavaScript.

# The Newsroom Design Lab

A finding says what is wrong. The lab shows what right could look like. Built 11 to 13 October 2026, it is four [SGit vaults](https://sgit.ai/), each a self-contained app, that try the fixes from the [newsroom review](/reviews/newsroom-2026-10-11.md) on the real newsroom data (a byte-faithful snapshot of 73 articles), **in three design directions each**, so that a direction can be chosen by looking rather than by arguing. Nothing in the lab changes the live site.

Every view in the lab says which step of the reader's path it moves them to: **arrive** through a link someone sent, **read** and rate, **come back**, **ask**, **act**.

## Three directions

A direction is a different design, not a recolour: different hierarchy, type, density and interaction, over the same data. Every vault has a switch in its top bar, and a Compare view that shows all three at phone width.

| Direction | The idea | Looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A · Broadsheet** | A serious publication. Editorial hierarchy, one lead, a named author with a stated purpose. | Serif headlines, warm paper, rules between columns, kickers, restrained colour. FT / Guardian long-read feel. |
| **B · Briefing** | Answers first. Every unit opens with the news in two sentences, then labelled blocks: the news, our view, the evidence, room for disagreement. | Sans, compact cards with reading time and format, bold labels, one accent colour. Semafor / Axios feel. |
| **C · Your desk** | The reader's own newsroom. The persona is the front page; the board, highlights, notes and questions are first-class. | App-like: left rail, side column, chips and progress. Readwise / Arc feel. |

## The same screen, three ways

## The decisions it exists to settle

The lab's hub vault lets the editor pick one option per decision, kept in the browser and downloadable as JSON. These are the questions, as the lab asks them.

1. **Which direction should the live front page take?** Everything else follows from it: type, density, how much the reader's own data shows. Options: A · Broadsheet; B · Briefing; C · Your desk; Mix: A for the publication, C for a signed-in reader.
2. **Which masthead line names the heart?** The tagline today describes a method, not a subject. Options: Field notes on AI agents, security and the next generation of publishing, by Dinis Cruz; Open thinking on agentic AI: what to build, how to secure it, and how to ship it; The agentic era, written in the open.
3. **How many doors on the first screen?** Three is easier to choose from; five covers everyone you send links to. Options: Three (security, builders, news); Five personas plus 'just looking'.
4. **What opens every article?** Readers have three minutes on a phone; the median article is about 4,500 words. Options: A boxed 'In brief' (the Explainer's short version); Labelled blocks: the news, our view, the evidence, room for disagreement; The article with the reader's side column.
5. **How should a rating reach you?** Today it stays in the reader's browser unless they send their whole reading. Options: One tap, anonymous, with plain consent; One tap, with an optional email for a reply; Kept locally, sent weekly with the reader's consent.
6. **Desks by audience or by subject?** Topics today overlap and one holds 38 of 73 articles. Options: Five desks by audience (proposed); Keep the six topics, add tag pages.
7. **Ship the reading board in the first release?** It gives a returning reader a reason to come back, and it is the most app-like piece. Options: Yes, on every persona page; Later, once ratings flow.

## What building the lab measured

Building apps that run inside the vault host turned up failures that are not about the newsroom at all: they are traps in the platform, and in the lab's own prototypes. They are in the register like any other finding.

- [UX-046](/findings/UX-046.md) · high · open · Setting location.hash inside a vault app re-navigates the frame: every link silently dead (dev.vault.sgraph.ai)
- [UX-047](/findings/UX-047.md) · medium · open · localStorage throws inside the vault app frame, so reader data is lost on reload (dev.vault.sgraph.ai)
- [UX-048](/findings/UX-048.md) · low · open · A vault app can load images and scripts from a site but cannot fetch its data (dev.vault.sgraph.ai)
- [UX-049](/findings/UX-049.md) · low · open · Query strings break inside the vault host, so filters must live in the route path (dev.vault.sgraph.ai)
- [UX-052](/findings/UX-052.md) · low · open · A highlight across paragraphs is cut at the first paragraph (Newsroom Design Lab)
- [UX-053](/findings/UX-053.md) · low · open · Search results show no snippets (Newsroom Design Lab)
- [UX-054](/findings/UX-054.md) · low · open · Stacked tables on a phone lose their column labels (Newsroom Design Lab)
- [UX-055](/findings/UX-055.md) · low · open · "Ask the article" has never run against a real on-device model (Newsroom Design Lab)
- [UX-050](/findings/UX-050.md) · medium · fixed · File-path pills scrolled the whole page sideways at 390 px (Newsroom Design Lab)
- [UX-051](/findings/UX-051.md) · medium · fixed · Re-rendering the whole view on every save lost the reader's place (Newsroom Design Lab)

## How it is built

A shared kit (v0.1.3, vendored into each vault): native web components with no framework, a bundler that packs each app into one `index.html` (the vault-app contract), an escaping template every view renders through, a router that never assigns `location.hash` inside the host, a reader store that uses the host's `sg.state` because the frame refuses `localStorage`, and a release gate that renders every route in every direction at 390 and 1280 px and fails on any page error, any colour outside the theme file, or any sideways scroll on a phone. Built by a lead with an architect agent and three developer agents, one vault each.

Reader data in the prototypes stays in the browser. Every "send" button is simulated, and says so, showing the receipt the real encrypted append lane would give.


==============================================================================
/method/  ·  /method/index.md
==============================================================================

# Method

A finding is only as good as its evidence. Everything here is measured on the live site, at a stated date and version, by someone using it as a stranger would. Opinion is welcome as long as it is labelled as one; the register holds what was seen.

## The reader's path

Every page is judged by which step it moves a reader to next. The path is the one the people these sites are written for actually take:

1. **Arrive** through a link someone sent, usually on a phone, with one question and a few minutes.
2. **Read** the first piece, and rate it.
3. **Come back**: a new pick, the newsletter, a reading board.
4. **Ask**: what is missing, a new version, a topic.
5. **Act**: try the product, start a conversation, put their own agents on a problem.

A finding is anything that stops a reader at one of these steps, or makes the next step harder than it needs to be.

## The stranger test

The cheapest test there is, and the one that finds most first-visit failures:

- Open the page on a phone (390×844), in a private window, with no history.
- Without scrolling: what is this, who is it for, and where do I go?
- Tap the first thing that looks like a way in. Did it go anywhere?
- Open the thing the site most wants you to read. How long is it? Did anything tell you before you opened it?
- Find every number. Is each one labelled, and do they agree with each other?

## The panel

A full review reads the same evidence through six roles, each with its own question. They disagree usefully: the Architect wanted the "For agents" strip on every page and the Designer wanted it off the first screen, and the answer (the page head and the footer) satisfied both.

| Role | The question it asks |
| --- | --- |
| Architect | Is there one pipeline, one source of truth, and URLs that will last? |
| Librarian | Can a reader find everything on a subject, and is the catalogue consistent? |
| Historian | Can a newcomer follow the arc of ideas from the start to now? |
| Designer | Does the first screen and the reading page serve a stranger on a phone? |
| Editor | Is the front page choosing for the reader, and is the voice consistent? |
| Journalist | Would a contact understand the story, trust it, and come back? |

Synthetic users (invented readers driven through the site by agents) add a seventh view, and a score that can be compared between releases. The newsroom's third run scored 2.4 out of 5; the next should add a CISO, who is most of the audience.

## Indexed nine ways

Every finding is indexed by **product** (whose fault it is), **area** (where in the visit), **problem** (what kind of thing goes wrong, one or more), **visibility** (how the reader experiences it), **recommendation** (the shape of the fix), **principle** (the rule it breaks), **severity**, **status** and **kind**. [Browse](/browse/index.md) shows every value of each with its count; the [findings list](/findings/index.md) filters by any combination, and the address is the filter.

| Visibility | Means |
| --- | --- |
| **Obvious** | Every reader sees it, every time they reach that point |
| **Intermittent** | Some readers, some of the time: depends on a gesture, a device or a state, and is hard to reproduce on demand |
| **Subtle** | Felt more than seen: costs attention or trust, but is not noticed as a bug |
| **Silent** | No symptom on screen: found only by measuring, or by its consequences |

Visibility is not severity. A silent failure (ratings that never reach anyone) can be the most serious on the site; an obvious one can be cosmetic. It says how a finding will be found, and therefore who will report it.

## Reports from readers

Most of the register will come from people using the sites and saying where they got stuck: a screenshot, a sentence, the page they were on. A report becomes a finding when it has been written up with the evidence, the device and browser, what the reader expected, and the fix, and indexed like any other. The report is the source; the finding page credits it.

A report about the browser rather than the page still goes in, with the browser as its product. Readers cannot tell whose fault a jumping toolbar is, and they blame the page they were reading, so knowing what the browser does is part of designing the page.

## What good looks like

When something gets it right, it is recorded as an [exemplar](/exemplars/index.md) in [/data/exemplars.json](/data/exemplars.json): what it does, why it works, what it still does not do, and which findings it answers. An exemplar is the best fix description there is, because it can be opened and tried.

## Failure or gap

| Kind | Means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Failure** | Something on the site works against the reader | Rating scales that start on 3; a balance that drops without notice |
| **Gap** | Something the reader needs is not there | No way to share a filtered list; no reading time on cards |

## Severity

| Severity | Means |
| --- | --- |
| **High** | Loses the reader, or the reader's trust, on the first visit. Or the site cannot learn from its readers at all |
| **Medium** | Costs the reader effort, or a return visit, or makes the site look unkept |
| **Low** | Polish and consistency: noticed by the careful, forgiven by most, fixed cheaply |

## Status, and what "checked" means

| Status | Means |
| --- | --- |
| **Open** | Still true when last checked |
| **Partly fixed** | Some of it changed; the finding says what is left |
| **Fixed** | No longer true, with the version that fixed it |

Every finding carries the date and version it was **observed** and the date and version it was **last checked**. A status is a claim about that date, not about today. Re-checking a finding means visiting it again, and updating both.

## Filing a finding

The register is one file, [/data/findings.json](/data/findings.json). A finding is one entry; the build turns it into a page, a markdown twin, a row in every list and filter, and a line in [llms.txt](/llms.txt). The fields:

```
{
 "id":        "UX-056",                       next free number, never reused
 "title":     "What is wrong, as a sentence",
 "product":   "newsroom.sgit.ai",             whose fault it is: a key of "products" in data/site.json
                                              (a site, the platform, a prototype, or a browser)
 "where":     "https://…/the/page.html",      the URL, or a description if there is none
 "area":      "first-visit",                  first-visit, navigation, findability, article,
                                              feedback, money, personas, trust, consistency, platform
 "problems":  ["unexpected-movement"],        one or more, from data/taxonomy.json
 "visibility": "intermittent",                obvious | intermittent | subtle | silent
 "recommendation": "keep-the-ui-still",       the shape of the fix, from data/taxonomy.json
 "kind":      "failure",                      failure | gap
 "severity":  "high",                         high | medium | low
 "status":    "open",                         open | partly-fixed | fixed
 "principle": "stranger-first-screen",        an id in data/principles.json
 "observed":  {"date": "2026-10-18", "version": "v0.7.3"},
 "checked":   {"date": "2026-10-18", "version": "v0.7.3"},
 "evidence":  "What was seen, measured: sizes, counts, the exact words on the page",
 "impact":    "Why it matters to the reader, in one or two sentences",
 "fix":       "The smallest change that removes it",
 "prototype": null,                           or {"vault": "newsroom-proto-front", "route": "front"}
 "source":    {"href": "/reviews/…", "label": "Where it was found"},
 "environment": "optional: device, browser, orientation, the page it happened on",
 "images":    [{"src": "/findings/img/UX-056-….webp", "alt": "…", "caption": "…"}],
 "status_note": "optional: what changed, and in which version"
}
```

Then `python3 admin/build/build.py` and `python3 admin/build/gate.py`. The gate fails on a missing field, an unknown site, area or principle, a duplicate id, a date that is not a date, a source link that goes nowhere, or a generated page that is out of date.

If a finding does not fit any [principle](/principles/index.md), add the principle: it earns its place by having a finding that breaks it.

## Rules for the register itself

- **Measure, then write.** Sizes, counts and the exact words on the page, not impressions of them.
- **Date every status.** A finding with no "last checked" is a rumour.
- **Name the fix.** A finding without a proposed fix is a complaint; the fix can be wrong, and that is fine.
- **Our own work is in scope.** The lab's prototypes and this site are reviewed like any other.
- **Content exists once.** The review is published whole and never edited; the register is where status changes.


==============================================================================
/principles/  ·  /principles/index.md
==============================================================================

# Principles

Each principle here is kept because at least one finding breaks it: the list grows from evidence, not from taste. Each has a test you can run on your own page in about a minute. When a new kind of failure does not fit any of them, that is a new principle.

1. [A decision comes with what you need to make it](/principles/index.md#informed-decisions)
2. [Work is never lost to one tap or a silent failure](/principles/index.md#work-is-never-lost)
3. [The reader can always tell what the system is doing](/principles/index.md#system-state-is-visible)
4. [The first screen is for a stranger](/principles/index.md#stranger-first-screen)
5. [Nothing moves that the reader did not move](/principles/index.md#ui-stays-still)
6. [The same gesture gives the same result, so it can be learned](/principles/index.md#same-gesture-same-result)
7. [Label the money, and never surprise with a charge](/principles/index.md#label-the-money)
8. [A default is not an answer](/principles/index.md#defaults-are-not-answers)
9. [Ask before keeping](/principles/index.md#ask-before-keeping)
10. [Every view is a link](/principles/index.md#every-view-is-a-link)
11. [No dead ends](/principles/index.md#no-dead-ends)
12. [One source of truth for every fact](/principles/index.md#one-source-of-truth)
13. [The publication is not the workshop](/principles/index.md#publication-not-workshop)
14. [Feedback reaches someone, and the reader gets a receipt](/principles/index.md#feedback-reaches-someone)
15. [Say how long, and what kind, before the reader commits](/principles/index.md#length-before-commitment)
16. [Say who wrote it, and how](/principles/index.md#say-who-wrote-it)
17. [Content is visible without waiting for scripts](/principles/index.md#content-is-visible)
18. [What a page says about the present is true now](/principles/index.md#state-is-current)
19. [A vault app works inside the host, not just on its own](/principles/index.md#host-safe-apps)

## 1. A decision comes with what you need to make it

**The rule.** Any prompt that asks the reader to decide (allow, pay, share, delete) first says, in plain words, what will happen, what it touches, whether it can be undone, and why it is being asked. The raw detail is there for checking, not as the explanation.

**Why.** A decision the reader cannot judge is not a decision. They either refuse and stall the work, or learn to press Allow without reading, and a security prompt that trains people to press Allow is worse than no prompt at all.

**The test.** Show the prompt to someone for five seconds. Can they say what will happen if they press each button? If they would need to read code to answer, the prompt has failed.

Broken by 2 findings, 2 open:

- [UX-059](/findings/UX-059.md) · open · A security prompt that asks you to approve a command it does not explain, and cuts off
- [UX-061](/findings/UX-061.md) · open · Three voice controls with no labels: the safe one and the send-as-is one sit side by side

## 2. Work is never lost to one tap or a silent failure

**The rule.** What the reader has made (a recording, a draft, a note) cannot be destroyed by a single unlabelled tap, and is kept when something fails. Destructive actions ask first or can be undone; failures keep the raw capture and offer a retry.

**Why.** Losing work once teaches the reader to distrust the whole tool. From then on they spend attention guarding against the tool instead of using it, and some stop using it at all.

**The test.** Make something, then press every button that could end the flow. Can any one tap destroy it without asking? Cut the network halfway: is what you made still there?

Broken by 1 findings, 1 open:

- [UX-060](/findings/UX-060.md) · open · One unlabelled X throws away the whole recording, with no confirmation

## 3. The reader can always tell what the system is doing

**The rule.** At every moment the interface shows whether it is listening, working, paused, done or failed. A process that stops shows that it stopped; it never just goes quiet.

**Why.** Silence is ambiguous. Without a visible state the reader cannot tell a slow system from a broken one, so they either wait for something that will never come or abandon something that was working.

**The test.** Start a long operation and watch it. If it stalled now, would anything on screen change? Can you tell "still working" from "failed" without waiting for the end?

Broken by 1 findings, 1 open:

- [UX-063](/findings/UX-063.md) · open · The live transcript sometimes stops while you are still speaking, and nothing says whether it is still recording

## 4. The first screen is for a stranger

**The rule.** On a phone, the first screen says what this is, who it is for, and where to go next. The lead is on it. Chrome, metadata and method come after.

**Why.** Most readers arrive from a link someone sent, on a phone, with one question and a few minutes. If the first screen does not answer 'what is this', the rest of the page is never read.

**The test.** Open the page at 390×844 with no history. Count the blocks above the lead. Can someone who has never heard of the site say what it is about?

Broken by 8 findings, 6 open:

- [UX-001](/findings/UX-001.md) · open · The first phone screen explains how the site is built, not what it is about
- [UX-002](/findings/UX-002.md) · open · The home page is 59 phone screens long, with 845 links
- [UX-017](/findings/UX-017.md) · open · There is no "start here" path
- [UX-045](/findings/UX-045.md) · open · Persona pages are a list, with no story, opinion or next step
- [UX-007](/findings/UX-007.md) · open · The editor's note is written for someone who read the last two editions
- [UX-054](/findings/UX-054.md) · open · Stacked tables on a phone lose their column labels
- [UX-003](/findings/UX-003.md) · fixed · The masthead line describes a method, not a subject
- [UX-050](/findings/UX-050.md) · fixed · File-path pills scrolled the whole page sideways at 390 px

## 5. Nothing moves that the reader did not move

**The rule.** While the reader is reading, the interface holds still. Toolbars, keyboards, banners and panels appear, move or take focus only on a deliberate gesture made for that purpose, never as a side effect of scrolling or reading.

**Why.** Movement pulls the eye. Every element that moves outside the reader's task forces a glance, a check and a return, which is a context switch the reader did not choose. On a reading page, concentration is the product.

**The test.** Read a long page on a phone or tablet: scroll down, scroll up a little, pause, carry on. Did anything appear, resize, shift or take focus that you did not ask for? Did the text you were reading stay where it was?

Broken by 3 findings, 2 open:

- [UX-056](/findings/UX-056.md) · open · Scrolling back up a little puts focus in the address bar and opens the keyboard
- [UX-057](/findings/UX-057.md) · open · The toolbars come back on any small scroll up, taking screen and moving the page
- [UX-051](/findings/UX-051.md) · fixed · Re-rendering the whole view on every save lost the reader's place

## 6. The same gesture gives the same result, so it can be learned

**The rule.** Every interaction behaves the same way every time, triggered by something the reader controls (where they tap, how far they scroll), never by something they cannot see or repeat (how fast they flicked, what state an animation was in).

**Why.** An interface teaches as it is used. When the same action always gives the same result, the reader learns it once and from then on can depend on it without thinking. When it depends on speed or timing, it can never be learned, and every use costs attention.

**The test.** Do the same thing five times: scroll, flick, tap, at slightly different speeds. Did the interface respond the same way each time? Could you reach the state you wanted on the first try?

Broken by 1 findings, 1 open:

- [UX-058](/findings/UX-058.md) · open · Whether the toolbars hide depends on how fast you scroll, not how far

## 7. Label the money, and never surprise with a charge

**The rule.** Every number that is money says what it is. The first time anything is charged, the reader is told before or as it happens. Wording about balances never reads as debt or threat.

**Why.** An unexplained balance that changes is read as a bill. One confused moment about money ends the visit and the trust.

**The test.** Find every currency figure on the page. Does each have a label? Open a page that charges: did anything say so?

Broken by 5 findings, 4 open:

- [UX-029](/findings/UX-029.md) · open · Opening an article charges a penny with no notice
- [UX-030](/findings/UX-030.md) · open · "Credit can go below zero" reads as a debt
- [UX-031](/findings/UX-031.md) · open · "You pay the price" reads as a warning
- [UX-028](/findings/UX-028.md) · partly fixed · The £5.00 balance chip has no label
- [UX-035](/findings/UX-035.md) · fixed · The top-up page said "simulated" while asking for money

## 8. A default is not an answer

**The rule.** Inputs that ask the reader's opinion start empty. Only what the reader actually did is recorded.

**Why.** A scale preset to 3 cannot tell 'not rated' from 'useful'. The data looks real and means nothing, to the reader and to the author.

**The test.** Open the form fresh. Is any answer already chosen? Submit without touching it: what was recorded?

Broken by 2 findings, 2 open:

- [UX-024](/findings/UX-024.md) · open · All three rating scales start on 3
- [UX-052](/findings/UX-052.md) · open · A highlight across paragraphs is cut at the first paragraph

## 9. Ask before keeping

**The rule.** Nothing is added to the reader's lists, profile or storage because they opened something. Keeping is a tap the reader makes.

**Why.** State the reader did not ask for is clutter at best and surveillance at worst. It also makes the reader's own record useless as a record.

**The test.** Open a page, close it. Did anything appear in the reader's list, board or persona set?

Broken by 2 findings, 2 open:

- [UX-027](/findings/UX-027.md) · open · Articles join the reader's list without being asked
- [UX-043](/findings/UX-043.md) · open · Opening a persona link adds it to the browser without asking

## 10. Every view is a link

**The rule.** Anything a reader can see, they can send: a filter, a search, a tag, a desk, a part of a series. The address changes when the view does.

**Why.** The people who most need a subset of the site are the ones a reader would forward it to. A view without an address cannot be shared, bookmarked or found by search.

**The test.** Choose a filter. Copy the address. Open it in a private window. Is it the same view?

Broken by 4 findings, 3 open:

- [UX-013](/findings/UX-013.md) · open · One topic holds more than half the articles
- [UX-015](/findings/UX-015.md) · open · Filters cannot be shared
- [UX-049](/findings/UX-049.md) · open · Query strings break inside the vault host, so filters must live in the route path
- [UX-042](/findings/UX-042.md) · fixed · Persona links were designed but not live

## 11. No dead ends

**The rule.** Everything that looks like a way in is one: tags link to pages, missing pages offer the way back, each article ends with one next step.

**Why.** A tag that does not link, a default 404 and an article that ends with seven options all stop the reader at the moment they were ready to go further.

**The test.** Click every pill, chip and label on a page. Visit a URL that does not exist. Reach the end of an article: what is the one next step?

Broken by 7 findings, 6 open:

- [UX-010](/findings/UX-010.md) · open · Missing pages show the default GitHub Pages 404
- [UX-014](/findings/UX-014.md) · open · Tags are not links, and there are no tag pages
- [UX-016](/findings/UX-016.md) · open · Series are invisible
- [UX-011](/findings/UX-011.md) · open · Links without extensions in one article
- [UX-012](/findings/UX-012.md) · open · Each article ends with seven next steps instead of one
- [UX-019](/findings/UX-019.md) · open · Search only matches titles, teasers and tags
- [UX-041](/findings/UX-041.md) · fixed · 51 vault images missing across 10 articles

## 12. One source of truth for every fact

**The rule.** Each piece of content is published once, at one canonical address. Every count, date and label is generated from one manifest at build time.

**Why.** Readers notice when two pages disagree, and they stop trusting both. A count that differs between three pages says the site does not know itself.

**The test.** Find the same number on three pages (article count, edition date, version). Do they agree? Does each article have exactly one canonical?

Broken by 4 findings, 3 open:

- [UX-037](/findings/UX-037.md) · open · Two domains claim to be canonical for the same article
- [UX-038](/findings/UX-038.md) · open · Three different article counts
- [UX-039](/findings/UX-039.md) · open · The feed is titled for the old site
- [UX-036](/findings/UX-036.md) · fixed · Articles were published on two domains, and diverged

## 13. The publication is not the workshop

**The rule.** Reader pages carry reader things. How the site is built (versions, author tooling, agent strips, release history, admin) lives in one clearly separate area, one link away.

**Why.** Builder chrome on a reader page spends the reader's attention on something they did not come for, and makes the site look like a demo instead of a publication.

**The test.** List every element on a reader page that only the author or an agent needs. Each one is a finding.

Broken by 4 findings, 4 open:

- [UX-009](/findings/UX-009.md) · open · Two navigation bars, and a 60-link menu that mixes reading with building
- [UX-005](/findings/UX-005.md) · open · The version number is shown three times on the first screen
- [UX-006](/findings/UX-006.md) · open · A "For agents /llms.txt" strip sits above the masthead
- [UX-021](/findings/UX-021.md) · open · Author tooling is shown to every reader

## 14. Feedback reaches someone, and the reader gets a receipt

**The rule.** Every rating, request or 'what is missing' goes somewhere a person reads it, by default and with plain consent, and the reader keeps a receipt of what was sent.

**Why.** Feedback kept only in the reader's browser teaches the author nothing, and a reader who is never answered stops answering.

**The test.** Rate something. Where did it go? Who reads it, and when? What does the reader have to show they sent it?

Broken by 3 findings, 3 open:

- [UX-025](/findings/UX-025.md) · open · Ratings never reach the author
- [UX-034](/findings/UX-034.md) · open · No contact for a pilot on the Replicate page
- [UX-026](/findings/UX-026.md) · open · There is no way to say what was missing

## 15. Say how long, and what kind, before the reader commits

**The rule.** Every card and every link to a long piece shows reading time and format. Every long piece opens with a short version.

**Why.** A reader with three minutes will not start a 25-minute piece blind. Telling them lets them choose; not telling them makes them leave.

**The test.** Look at a list of articles. Can you tell which is a five-minute note and which is a 40-minute analysis?

Broken by 3 findings, 3 open:

- [UX-018](/findings/UX-018.md) · open · Cards do not show reading time or format
- [UX-020](/findings/UX-020.md) · open · The best reader feature is buried under metadata and a long italic abstract
- [UX-053](/findings/UX-053.md) · open · Search results show no snippets

## 16. Say who wrote it, and how

**The rule.** The byline names the person and the way the piece was made (with agents, from voice notes), where the reader looks, not in the footer. The purpose of the publication is one link away.

**Why.** Readers judge a piece by who stands behind it. Disclosure in the footer reads as concealment when it is found.

**The test.** From the top of any article, can a reader tell who wrote it, with what help, and why the publication exists?

Broken by 4 findings, 4 open:

- [UX-033](/findings/UX-033.md) · open · It is unclear how a writer gets paid
- [UX-022](/findings/UX-022.md) · open · The byline names one human; the AI authorship is in the footer
- [UX-023](/findings/UX-023.md) · open · There is no page that says why the publication exists
- [UX-062](/findings/UX-062.md) · open · The transcript is cleaned up in a second pass without saying when, or what changed

## 17. Content is visible without waiting for scripts

**The rule.** The page renders its content in HTML and shows it at once. Scripts enhance; they never gate what the reader can see.

**Why.** A blank page for a second and a half on a slow phone is the page, for that reader. Agents, readers and search engines that do not run scripts see nothing.

**The test.** Load the page with JavaScript off, and on a throttled connection. Is the content there at once?

Broken by 2 findings, 2 open:

- [UX-044](/findings/UX-044.md) · open · The founder page says "the picks above" and no picks render on a phone
- [UX-008](/findings/UX-008.md) · open · Content is hidden until JavaScript runs

## 18. What a page says about the present is true now

**The rule.** Labels like 'edition of', 'currently', 'broken' and 'live' are dated or generated, and change when the facts do. A fixed problem is marked fixed, with the version.

**Why.** A page that describes a fixed bug as current, or labels today's front page with last week's date, tells the reader the rest may be stale too.

**The test.** Find every claim about now on the page. Is each dated? Is each still true?

Broken by 4 findings, 3 open:

- [UX-032](/findings/UX-032.md) · open · Nothing shows real money moving
- [UX-040](/findings/UX-040.md) · open · The study page reports a fixed bug as current
- [UX-055](/findings/UX-055.md) · open · "Ask the article" has never run against a real on-device model
- [UX-004](/findings/UX-004.md) · fixed · The edition label is older than the articles under it

## 19. A vault app works inside the host, not just on its own

**The rule.** An app is tested where readers open it: inside the vault host's sandboxed frame. Routing never assigns location.hash, storage goes through the host, and network reads come from the vault.

**Why.** The host frame behaves unlike a normal page. An app that works standalone can ship with every link dead and every saved note lost on reload.

**The test.** Open the published vault in the host, click every link, save something, reload. Check the console.

Broken by 3 findings, 3 open:

- [UX-046](/findings/UX-046.md) · open · Setting location.hash inside a vault app re-navigates the frame: every link silently dead
- [UX-047](/findings/UX-047.md) · open · localStorage throws inside the vault app frame, so reader data is lost on reload
- [UX-048](/findings/UX-048.md) · open · A vault app can load images and scripts from a site but cannot fetch its data
